title: The stolen pears (Confessions 2)
hook: Augustine remembers stealing pears as a boy, not from hunger, just to do wrong

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jerome's Bible, the Vulgate, and your line was ignorance of scripture is ignorance of christ. Which word did you catch a translator choosing? Day seven hundred seventy-nine.
screen: `IGNORANCE OF SCRIPTURE IS IGNORANCE OF CHRIST.`

segments.voice: It's late at night, and a gang of boys has stayed out in the streets longer than they should. Near a vineyard stands a pear tree, loaded with fruit. The pears aren't much to look at, and not much to taste. The boys shake the tree anyway and carry off armfuls. They eat a few. The rest they throw to the pigs. One of those boys grew up to be Augustine, and years later, writing his Confessions, he could not let that night go. He kept asking one question about it. Today: the stolen pears.

The Confessions is a long prayer. Augustine tells his life to God, out loud, on the page. And of everything he could linger on, he stops at a pear tree. Why? Because, he says, he wasn't hungry. He had better pears at home. He didn't want the fruit. He wanted the stealing. He loved, he says, the wrong itself. That honesty is the strange gift of this chapter. It's easy to explain small wrongs away: I was tired, I was provoked, everybody does it. Augustine refuses the excuse. He looks for the reason, and keeps looking, and the first answer he finds is ugly: he did it because it wasn't allowed. Then he finds a second. He would not, he says, have done it alone. It was the company: the laughing, the daring, the not wanting to be the one who held back. He calls it a friendship that was no friend at all. That's the turn. The theft wasn't only about pears. It was about belonging. Paul had put words to this tangle in his letter to the Romans: "for what I would, that do I not; but what I hate, that do I." Augustine gives a boyhood prank his full attention because he's digging for the root. Readers take the chapter in more than one way. Some connect it with Augustine's later teaching on the bent of the human will and on original sin. Others read it more simply, as a man telling the truth about a night he'd rather forget. Either way, he doesn't stop at the guilt. The whole book is spoken to the God he believes forgave him. Naming the wrong is the first step. Finding the reason is the second.

Here's the practice: remember a small wrong, honestly. Settle, and breathe. Let one small wrong from long ago come to mind, nothing heavy: something taken, a lie told, a cruelty you joined in. Don't defend it, and don't punish yourself with it. Just ask Augustine's question. Why did I do it? Was it the thing itself, or the doing, or the people watching? Let the real answer come up slowly. If you pray, you can tell God the reason you find. If you don't, simply let yourself know it, for this minute. The bell holds the time.
The stolen pears. Augustine's boyhood theft, done not from hunger, but for the wrong itself, and for the company.
Your line: know why you do it. Today, before one small choice, a purchase, a reply, a joke at someone's expense, pause and ask the reason underneath. Day seven hundred seventy-nine.

howItsDone: Augustine's Confessions is read by Christians of different churches as a model of honest self-examination; some use the practice of examining the day, or the examination of conscience before confession, in the same spirit.

fork.setup: you're Augustine, years later, looking back at the pear tree. why did you do it?
options: I loved the wrong itself, and I wouldn't have done it alone.
fork.reveal: he wasn't hungry and didn't want the fruit. he found two reasons: the wrong itself, and the friends who were with him.

original.note: Greek: sin. Paul's word in Romans 7 for the thing he says dwells in him.

trapdoor: what you thought: a boy stole some fruit. no big deal.
what it means: Augustine uses a small theft to ask why people do wrong at all, and finds the wrong itself, and the group.
what a scholar hears: the Confessions is addressed to God throughout, and some readers connect the pear tree with Augustine's later teaching on the will and original sin.

notes: Confessions 2.4.9: pear tree near the vineyard, fruit not tempting, late at night after games in the streets, carried off loads, ate a few, threw the rest to the pigs; he had better at home; he loved the wrong itself. Paraphrased (Pusey 1838 is public domain but not quoted, to avoid misquoting). Confirm.
Confessions 2.8.16–2.9.17: he would not have done it alone; 'O friendship too unfriendly' paraphrased as 'a friendship that was no friend at all'. Confirm.
No age is given (Confessions 2.3.6 places this in his sixteenth year; omitted under the claims rule).
The two readings (link to original sin / plain honest memory) are attributed to 'some' readers and not ranked; confirm fairness to Orthodox readers, who frame ancestral sin differently.
Audit: cut 'Augustine isn't trying to make a boyhood prank sound monstrous' (he calls the act foul and dwells on it at length; the line misread his tone).
